history.heading: Kalinago stronghold
paragraphs: Dominica, a mountainous volcanic island in the eastern Caribbean, was inhabited by the Kalinago (Island Caribs), who named it Wai'tu kubuli, meaning "tall is her body". Columbus sighted it on a Sunday in 1493 and named it after the day. Its rugged terrain allowed the Kalinago to resist European colonisation longer than elsewhere.

history.heading: Colonial rivalry and independence
paragraphs: France and Britain contested the island in the 18th century; Britain gained control in 1763. Plantations of coffee and sugar used enslaved Africans, while escaped slaves, called maroons, formed communities in the interior. Slavery was abolished in 1834.
Dominica became independent on 3 November 1978. Eugenia Charles, prime minister from 1980 to 1995, was the Caribbean's first female head of government. Hurricane Maria devastated the island in 2017.

culture.heading: Nature island culture
paragraphs: English is official, and Kwéyòl, a French-based Creole, is widely spoken. Most people are Catholic. Dominica is home to the Kalinago Territory, where descendants of the island's original inhabitants live.
The World Creole Music Festival celebrates genres such as bouyon. Callaloo soup and mountain chicken (a large frog, now endangered) are traditional foods.

politics.heading: Parliamentary republic
paragraphs: Dominica is a parliamentary republic and member of the Commonwealth. The president is elected by parliament as head of state, while the prime minister leads the government. The Dominica Labour Party has governed since 2000.

economy.heading: Agriculture and ecotourism
paragraphs: Bananas were once the main export but have declined. The economy relies on agriculture, ecotourism, attracted by rainforests, hot springs and the Boiling Lake, and a citizenship-by-investment programme that funds much public spending. Dominica aims to become the world's first climate-resilient nation. The currency is the Eastern Caribbean dollar.
